PAPERS.title: What Does Sensor Performance Really Mean? A Four-Layer Framework for Interpreting Air Quality Sensor Performance Evaluations.
PAPERS.short: Malings group four-layer framework for reading air-quality sensor performance evaluations (who, what product, what context, what metrics)
PAPERS.pm: Fixed outdoor air-quality sensors (PM and gases); evaluation metrics as reported in sensor performance evaluations
PAPERS.endpoint: Interpretability of sensor performance claims (no measured endpoint)
PAPERS.affil: Universidad del Desarrollo, Chile; TD Environmental Services, USA
PAPERS.n: Conceptual framework for interpreting sensor performance evaluations (SPEs) of fixed outdoor air-quality sensors, built on four questions: who led the evaluation, which data product was evaluated (raw, manufacturer-corrected, user-calibrated, cloud-processed), in what context (site, season, concentration range, co-location length), and what the metrics do and do not convey. It yields guiding questions that separate missing from uncertain information instead of ranking devices on headline R2 or RMSE. It does not set fitness-for-purpose thresholds and adds no co-location data, so its value depends on uptake by evaluators. Relevance: direct - this is the reporting layer every low-cost PM calibration paper needs; 'which data product' is the question most often left implicit behind published R2 values.

PAPERS.title: Toxicity-Weighted Assessment Reveals the Rising Dominance of Non-Exhaust PM2.5 from On-Road Transportation in China
PAPERS.short: Fudan non-exhaust (brake + tire) PM2.5 5-11x more toxic per mass than exhaust; toxicity-adjusted share 54% (2014) to 96% (2050) in China
PAPERS.pm: Dynamometer-generated brake/tyre-wear and exhaust PM2.5; oxidative stress and cytotoxicity potencies combined with emission inventories
PAPERS.endpoint: Toxicity-adjusted on-road PM2.5 emissions and exposure hotspots
PAPERS.affil: Fudan University, China; Fudan University, China
PAPERS.n: Dynamometer tests, chemical analysis and in vitro assays gave non-exhaust (brake and tyre wear) PM2.5 oxidative-stress and cytotoxicity potencies 5- to 11-fold higher per unit mass than exhaust PM2.5. Weighting Chinese on-road inventories by these potencies, toxicity-adjusted non-exhaust emissions in 2023 were about eight times exhaust; the non-exhaust share is projected to rise from 54% (2014) to 96% (2050) under electrification without dedicated controls. Weakness: the potency ratio comes from a small set of pads, tyres and engines under dynamometer conditions and in vitro endpoints, then is applied nationally with no reported uncertainty. Relevance: mass-based optical sensors cannot see this shift; a toxicity-weighted burden argues for composition or oxidative-potential proxies near roads.

PAPERS.title: Exposure to specific particulate matter (PM) sources and constituents are differentially associated with circulating immune biomarkers in women.
PAPERS.short: California Teachers Study 1898 women: source/component PM0.1-PM10 and 15 immune markers; 12-mo PM2.5 EC with IL-1b, sCD27, sTNFR2
PAPERS.pm: Source- and component-resolved PM0.1, PM2.5 and PM10 at residence (modelling method not stated in abstract); 1-, 3- and 12-month means per IQR
PAPERS.endpoint: Quartiles of 15 circulating immune markers (IL-1b, sCD27, sTNFR2, IL-8, CCL2, sgp130 and others)
PAPERS.affil: Beckman Research Institute, City of Hope, USA; University of California, Davis, USA
PAPERS.n: 1,898 California Teachers Study women, blood drawn 2015; residential source- and component-resolved PM0.1, PM2.5 and PM10 at 1-, 3- and 12-month lags, multinomial models per IQR, Bonferroni-corrected. PM2.5 elemental carbon was associated with top-quartile IL-1b (12-month OR 2.95, 95% CI 1.94-4.48), sCD27 (2.05, 1.34-3.13) and sTNFR2 (2.70, 1.73-4.21) at every lag; PM10 off-road diesel with IL-8 (OR 1.68, 1.23-2.30) and CCL2. PM2.5 copper and PM0.1 biomass were inversely associated with sgp130, sTNFR2 and sCD27. Weakness: one blood draw, so cross-sectional; many source x marker x lag tests; modelled component surfaces with correlated errors. Relevance: EC, the component most tractable for low-cost absorption measurement, carries the strongest immune signal.

PAPERS.title: Size-Divergent Contributors and Interactions to PM Oxidative Potential: EC-Organics Additivity and Ion-Metal Synergy.
PAPERS.short: Nankai nine-stage size-resolved PM oxidative potential: fine OP from EC + 9,10-PQ (additive), coarse OP from bioaccessible metals, ion-metal synergy
PAPERS.pm: Size-resolved PM in nine cascade-impactor stages; ~100 components incl. bioaccessible fractions in simulated epithelial lung fluid; DTT oxidative potential
PAPERS.endpoint: DTT oxidative potential (OPv) by size fraction and source (PMF + XGBoost-SHAP)
PAPERS.affil: Nankai University, China; Nankai University, China
PAPERS.n: Cascade-impactor PM in nine size fractions; ~100 components measured as ambient and lung-fluid bioaccessible concentrations, with DTT oxidative potential. Fine-particle OP was driven by elemental carbon, 9,10-phenanthrenequinone and ions, with laboratory confirmation that EC and 9,10-PQ act additively; coarse OP was dominated by bioaccessible Ni, Cu, As and Mn, ions raising OP by increasing metal bioaccessibility. PMF plus XGBoost-SHAP ranked traffic, secondary aerosol and combustion below 2.1 um, traffic and dust at 3.3-10 um. The abstract gives no sampling period, site count or effect sizes. Weakness: DTT is one acellular assay with metal-organic interferences, and SHAP importance is not source causality. Relevance: mass-only sensing misranks coarse-mode hazard; size matters beyond PM2.5.

PAPERS.title: Stage-resolved PM(2.5), PM(10), and VOC concentrations during field-simulated ski waxing and tuning: A pilot study with an exploratory worker survey.
PAPERS.short: Utah ski-waxing pilot with low-cost optical PM sensor + PID: application stage PM2.5 456-771 ug/m3; 8% of 50 workers have dedicated exhaust
PAPERS.pm: Near-field PM2.5 and PM10 from a low-cost optical sensor, total VOC from a PID, by waxing/tuning stage
PAPERS.endpoint: Stage-resolved PM2.5, PM10 and TVOC concentrations; worker survey on wax type and ventilation
PAPERS.affil: University of Utah, USA; University of Utah, USA
PAPERS.n: Two-phase pilot: survey of 50 ski-industry workers (69.2% of those knowing their wax used fluorocarbon wax; 8% had effective dedicated exhaust) and field-simulated waxing and tuning with three block waxes over four stages, measured with a low-cost optical PM sensor and a PID. Wax application gave the highest run-level means, PM2.5 about 456-771 ug/m3 and PM10 602-1,045 ug/m3; brushing and scraping were intermediate; ironing raised PM only for the fluorinated race wax at 160 C; tuning was far lower. Weakness: wax type and iron temperature are confounded, the sensor was not reported as gravimetrically corrected for wax aerosol, and runs are few. Relevance: a clean case of an LCS used for stage-resolved occupational profiling, where the uncorrected mass scale is the main threat.

PAPERS.title: Exposure to particulate matter, black carbon, and ultrafine particles at Philadelphia subway stations.
PAPERS.short: Villanova Philadelphia subway: belowground PM2.5 5.1x, BC 16.5x, UFP LDSA 1.9x street level; 15th St PM2.5 157 ug/m3
PAPERS.pm: Concurrent belowground and street-level PM2.5, black carbon and ultrafine lung-deposited surface area at three stations
PAPERS.endpoint: Microenvironment concentration ratios; PM2.5 risk quotient
PAPERS.affil: Villanova University, USA; Villanova University, USA
PAPERS.n: Concurrent belowground and street-level measurements at three Philadelphia subway stations, summer 2023. Belowground means exceeded street level about 5.1x for PM2.5, 16.5x for black carbon and 1.9x for UFP lung-deposited surface area; 15th Street was highest (PM2.5 156.8 +/- 25.3 ug/m3; LDSA 56.7 +/- 21.2 um2/cm3). A PM2.5 risk quotient below 1 was reported for commuters. Weakness: one season, three stations, no instrument models in the abstract; iron-rich subway PM makes optical mass ambient-calibrated instruments unreliable, and the low-risk conclusion rests on commuter-duration averaging and ignores workers. Relevance: subway platforms are a microenvironment where personal and low-cost monitors read high and need aerosol-specific correction.

PAPERS.title: Internet of Things (IoT) in environmental public health: Monitoring environmental hazards and supporting public health action.
PAPERS.short: North South University structured narrative review of 45 sources on IoT in environmental public health; PM2.5 sensing most mature
PAPERS.pm: IoT environmental sensors, chiefly PM2.5 low-cost networks; ML calibration and drift
PAPERS.endpoint: Evidence maturity across sensor performance, exposure characterisation, early warning and health impact
PAPERS.affil: North South University, Bangladesh; North South University, Bangladesh
PAPERS.n: Structured narrative review of 45 sources (PubMed/PMC, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, citation tracking) grading IoT environmental-health evidence by maturity across technical validity, data quality, interoperability, security, privacy, equity, cost and public-health utility. Evidence is strongest for field-validated PM2.5 sensing and exposure characterisation; ML calibration reduces drift when retrained across seasons or networks, but transfer is pollutant- and site-dependent; evidence that automated sensor alerts improve population health is scant. Weakness: single-author synthesis of a small, non-systematic source set with no risk-of-bias assessment, so maturity grades are judgement. Relevance: restates the gap this watch keeps finding - networks are validated as instruments, almost never as interventions with measured health or behavioural outcomes.

PAPERS.title: Chemical Characterization and Source Apportionment of PM2.5 During Autumn and Winter in an Industrial High-Tech Zone of the Yangtze River Delta, China
PAPERS.short: Nanjing Institute YRD industrial high-tech zone autumn-winter PM2.5 PMF: industry 39.6%, mobile 14.6%, ammonium nitrate drives episodes
PAPERS.pm: Filter PM2.5 water-soluble ions and constituents, Nov 2024-Jan 2025; PMF with secondary reallocation by inventory
PAPERS.endpoint: Source contributions to PM2.5; SOR/NOR
PAPERS.affil: Nanjing Institute of Environmental Sciences, China; Nanjing Institute of Environmental Sciences, China
PAPERS.n: Intensive PM2.5 sampling in an industrial high-tech zone of the western Yangtze River Delta, November 2024-January 2025. Nitrate, sulfate and ammonium made up 62.8-91% of water-soluble ions; mean SOR 0.365, NOR 0.207; NH4+ and NO3- rose significantly from clean to polluted periods, implicating ammonium nitrate. PMF resolved seven factors; after reallocating secondary aerosol to primary sources via the local inventory, industry contributed 39.6%, mobile 14.6%, fugitive dust 11.9%, cooking 11.9%, coal 11.4%. Weakness: one site, one season, and the reallocation step imports inventory assumptions, so the industrial share is partly model-defined. Relevance: nitrate-driven episodes are where hygroscopic-growth errors in optical sensors peak, so this composition context matters for any local network.

PAPERS.title: Estimation of spatio-temporal air pollutant emissions from wheat residue burning in the Central Part of India.
PAPERS.short: NIT Raipur VIIRS FRP-based wheat-residue burning emissions, Madhya Pradesh 2019-2023: 130,766 fires, PM2.5 peak 0.9 Gg (2022)
PAPERS.pm: FRP-based emissions of CO2, CO, PM2.5, OC and EC from VIIRS NOAA-20 active fires masked by SPAM wheat and ESA WorldCover
PAPERS.endpoint: District-level emissions and hotspots; HYSPLIT transport pathways
PAPERS.affil: National Institute of Technology Raipur, India; National Institute of Technology Raipur, India
PAPERS.n: VIIRS NOAA-20 active fires (130,766 detections after wheat and cropland masking) converted to fire-radiative-power emissions for Madhya Pradesh, 2019-2023. State CO2 ranged 111-161 Gg per year; 2022 peaked with PM2.5 0.9 Gg, OC 0.3 Gg and EC 0.2 Gg; Hoshangabad, Raisen and Vidisha were persistent hotspots; burning concentrated in March-May; HYSPLIT traced transport pathways. Weakness: FRP emission coefficients are not locally validated, small and cloud-obscured fires are missed (the authors call totals lower bounds), and there is no comparison with ground PM. Relevance: indirect - a source inventory for post-harvest burning in central India, where ground monitoring is thin; a distributed sensor network would be the missing check on satellite-derived timing and magnitude.

PAPERS.journal: J Environ Sci Health A Tox Hazard Subst Environ Eng
PAPERS.title: Assessment of air quality and heavy metals in residential and commercial areas of Aizawl and Lawngtlai districts, Mizoram.
PAPERS.short: Mizoram (Aizawl, Lawngtlai) 2023-2024 fire period: PM10 74 vs 50 ug/m3; breathing difficulty 44% vs 12% between districts
PAPERS.pm: Ambient PM10, PM2.5, SPM, gases and heavy metals at residential and commercial sites, site x year x month means
PAPERS.endpoint: Fire vs non-fire concentrations; self-reported respiratory symptoms (n=261)
PAPERS.affil: Mizoram University, India; Pachhunga University College, India
PAPERS.n: Ambient monitoring at residential and commercial sites in Aizawl and Lawngtlai, Mizoram, 2023-2024, aggregated to site-month means, plus a symptom survey of 261 respondents. In the February-March fire period PM10 was 74.20 vs 50.35 ug/m3 (P=0.03) and SPM 131.25 vs 84.70 ug/m3 (P=0.02); PM2.5 31.85 vs 26.69 ug/m3 was method-sensitive (Welch P=0.08, Mann-Whitney P=0.02). Breathing difficulty in the fire period: 43.82% in Aizawl vs 12.00% in Lawngtlai. Weakness: few sites, monthly aggregates and no respondent-level exposure, so the symptom contrast is between districts, not exposures. Relevance: northeast India has almost no continuous monitoring; seasonal fire PM is the signal a low-cost network would resolve daily.

PAPERS.title: Environmental footprint of armed conflict in the Gaza Strip: A remote sensing assessment of air, water, and land-use dynamic.
PAPERS.short: Mansoura/NIOF multi-sensor remote-sensing footprint of the Gaza conflict 2022-2025: aerosol loading up, land-use and water degraded
PAPERS.pm: MODIS aerosol loading (AOD) and thermal anomalies alongside Sentinel/Landsat land cover and VIIRS night lights
PAPERS.endpoint: Change in aerosol indicators, LULC, vegetation and water quality pre-conflict vs conflict
PAPERS.affil: Mansoura University, Egypt; National Institute of Oceanography and Fisheries, Egypt
PAPERS.n: Multi-sensor satellite time series (Sentinel-1/2, Landsat 8/9, MODIS, VIIRS) for the Gaza Strip, 2022-2025, quantifying land-use change, vegetation loss, surface-water extent and quality proxies, infrastructure disruption, and atmospheric impact via aerosol loading and thermal anomalies. The abstract reports increased atmospheric pollution indicators during the conflict but gives no AOD magnitude, trend or uncertainty. Weakness: column AOD over a strip of about 365 km2 is dominated by regional dust and marine aerosol, so attribution to the conflict without a control region or meteorological adjustment is not established; no surface PM is estimated. Relevance: low-moderate - where in situ monitoring is impossible, this shows the limits of AOD-only inference and the case for rapidly deployable sensors in crises.

PAPERS.title: In vivo inhalation toxicity of polystyrene nanoplastic particles: PSLT-like responses of apical endpoints and transcriptomic changes
PAPERS.short: Nose-only 28-d rat inhalation of respirable polystyrene nanoplastic agglomerates: overload-type lung effects at 50 not 5 mg/m3
PAPERS.pm: Respirable polystyrene particle agglomerates, nose-only 5 and 50 mg/m3, 6 h/d, 5 d/wk, 28 d; 5 and 13 wk recovery
PAPERS.endpoint: BALF, histopathology, lung and liver transcriptomics
PAPERS.affil: not stated in record; not stated in record
PAPERS.n: Male Wistar rats exposed nose-only to respirable polystyrene agglomerates at 5 and 50 mg/m3 for 28 days, with about 5 and 13 weeks recovery. At 50 mg/m3: neutrophilic infiltration, type II pneumocyte and bronchiolo-alveolar hyperplasia, raised lung weight and persistent particle-associated changes - an overload profile typical of poorly soluble low-toxicity particles. At 5 mg/m3 no adverse apical effects, though lung transcripts in complement, coagulation and lipid pathways shifted; liver changes were minimal. Weakness: one polymer and particle form, male rats only, doses orders of magnitude above ambient airborne microplastic levels. Relevance: indirect - supports treating inhaled low-reactivity plastic particles within the PSLT mass-dose framework rather than as a unique hazard.

PAPERS.title: Heat stress and air pollution in female reproductive health: from pathological alterations to molecular mechanisms
PAPERS.short: Harbin narrative review: heat stress and air pollution in female reproductive health, ovarian reserve to placentation, oxidative stress mechanisms
PAPERS.pm: Ambient air pollution including PM2.5 and PM10 as reported by source studies; exposure metrics heterogeneous
PAPERS.endpoint: Ovarian reserve, implantation, live birth, pregnancy loss, preterm birth, hypertensive disorders
PAPERS.affil: First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University, China; First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University, China
PAPERS.n: Narrative review of epidemiological, pathological and mechanistic evidence on heat and air pollution in female reproduction. Epidemiology links both to diminished ovarian reserve, lower implantation and live-birth rates, pregnancy loss, preterm birth and hypertensive disorders; pathology to impaired folliculogenesis, defective spiral-artery remodelling and endometrial receptivity; mechanisms to oxidative stress, inflammation, epigenetic reprogramming, apoptosis and autophagy. The authors name heterogeneous exposure assessment and poorly defined susceptible windows as the main limits. Weakness: no search strategy or quantitative synthesis, and heat and PM evidence are merged, so no PM-specific dose-response can be extracted. Relevance: low - but the stated bottleneck, exposure in narrow windows such as peri-implantation, is what personal or residential sensing addresses.

PAPERS.title: Dust Storms as Dynamic Multipollutant Exposure Systems: Environmental Transformation, Toxicological Mechanisms, and Health Implications
PAPERS.short: Zhejiang Normal/RCEES review: dust storms as dynamic multipollutant exposure systems - transformation, toxicology, health
PAPERS.pm: Mineral dust PM with adsorbed anthropogenic pollutants, metals, microbes and secondary coatings
PAPERS.endpoint: Health effects of dust events; toxicological mechanisms
PAPERS.affil: Zhejiang Normal University, China; Research Center for Eco-Environmental Sciences, CAS, China
PAPERS.n: Review reframing dust storms as dynamic multipollutant exposure systems: mineral particles acquire anthropogenic and secondary components during transport, so toxicity reflects coatings, metals and biological content rather than crustal mass alone. It integrates environmental chemistry, exposure science, toxicology and epidemiology to propose a basis for dust-specific health risk assessment. The abstract gives no search method, quantitative synthesis or effect estimates. Weakness: conceptual; the claim that transport-aged dust is more toxic per unit mass is plausible but not quantified here. Relevance: moderate - optical low-cost sensors undercount coarse dust and mass alone misses ageing, so dust events are where calibration and toxicity weighting fail together.

PAPERS.title: Emerging inhalation risks: Global distribution of airborne algal and cyanobacterial toxins.
PAPERS.short: Ohio State review of 27 studies: aerosolised algal and cyanobacterial toxins - microcystin up to 40 ng/m3, brevetoxin, BMAA
PAPERS.pm: Aerosolised harmful-algal-bloom toxins sampled by filters, cascade impactors and impingers
PAPERS.endpoint: Toxin detection and concentration in aerosol; inhalation health effects
PAPERS.affil: The Ohio State University, USA; The Ohio State University, USA
PAPERS.n: Review of 27 studies across North America, Europe, Asia and Oceania on aerosolised harmful algal and cyanobacterial bloom toxins. Fourteen toxins were detected in aerosol; microcystin appeared in 41% of studies (marine and freshwater, maximum 40.0 ng/m3), brevetoxin in 37% (all marine), BMAA in 11%. Sampling (filters, cascade impactors, impingers) and analysis (ELISA, LC-MS/MS, LC-HRMS) differ widely; transport of kilometres to hundreds of kilometres inland is reported. Weakness: few studies with incomparable methods, no exposure-response data, and size distributions of toxin-bearing aerosol rarely reported. Relevance: a bioaerosol pathway invisible to mass-based PM monitoring; size-resolved sampling near bloom waters is the missing measurement layer.
